errors.english: This is not the case; if it were to possess parts
errors.why: de lta ma yin te here means 'otherwise': if it had parts it would not be substantially existent, which supports the preceding claim that it must be partless rather than denying it.

errors.english: In order to demonstrate the meaning of the scripture
errors.why: mdo here is the root verse (kārikā) being commented on, not scripture; the note's 'or Dharmakirti' is also misleading, since the root text is Dignāga's.

errors.english: Because the cognition of that appearance would perish, it is said that this appearance in cognition is...
errors.why: The root line 'because the cognition appearing as that would be lost' is quoted as a lemma, and the commentary begins glossing it ('since this cognition has such an appearance, it is...'); the English merges lemma and gloss into one sentence.

note: A sound rendering of the argument against differentiated atoms; a few slips in how the commentary handles its root text.

errors.english: it is affected by the transformative power of the object or the sense faculties
errors.why: It is the object or the sense faculty that is altered by a (supernatural) empowerment, not the power of the object or faculty that affects something.

fix.find: it is affected by the transformative power of the object or the sense faculties
fix.replace: the object or the sense faculty is affected by a transformative power

errors.english: the object of cognition and the negation of that object are designated as existing because they are present
errors.why: dgag par bya ba is the negandum: the cognition and its object, which are what is to be negated, are existent in the sense of being designated as existent; nothing here is 'the negation of that object'.

fix.find: the object of cognition and the negation of that object are designated as existing because they are present
fix.replace: the cognition and its object, which are what is to be negated, are existent in the sense of being designated as existent

errors.english: while their reversal is the non-existence of non-perception. Thus, even the perceived is said to be non-existent.
errors.why: Their absence is non-existence in the form of non-perception, which is why it is called 'absence of perception' (anupalabdhi); it does not say the non-existence of non-perception, nor that the perceived is non-existent.

errors.english: other qualifying characteristics such as the dewlap will be explained after the characteristics of the cow are reversed
errors.why: It says that other things having a ground (nimittin) will be explained [as negated] through the absence of their ground, as 'cow' is negated through the absence of its marks, the dewlap etc.

errors.english: by using signs that are not incompatible with the body or the mind
errors.why: Body and mind are the Mīmāṃsakas' signs, which are not incompatible with omniscience etc.; the English makes them what the signs fail to contradict.

fix.find: by using signs that are not incompatible with the body or the mind
fix.replace: by using signs such as having a body and a mind, which are not incompatible with omniscience and so forth

note: The overall shape of the discussion of non-perception is followed, but several key clauses (adhiṣṭhāna, the negandum, the Mīmāṃsaka signs) are misconstrued.

errors.english: the *Sub-commentary on the Requests* [note: original: "Zhu ba" / Vinayaupayika]
errors.why: Zhu ba is the canonical Vinaya 'Questions' (the questions section of the Uttaragrantha), cited as scripture; it is not a sub-commentary, and 'Vinayaupayika' is wrong.

fix.find: the *Sub-commentary on the Requests* [note: original: "Zhu ba" / Vinayaupayika]
fix.replace: the *Questions* (*Zhu ba*) [note: the questions section of the Vinaya Uttaragrantha]

errors.english: [note: the person responsible for the action leading to a transgression]
errors.why: byed pa po nyid here is the factor that constitutes the offence, and the answer given is the vihāra, not a person; the note (and 'makes one a maker' below) misleads.

errors.english: Since there is no specific distinction made, it is understood that the monastery is currently under the authority of the household
errors.why: It says that because the qualifier 'one who now has authority over a house' is not stated, the rule is understood to apply to vihāras too, in all cases; it does not assert the monastery is under a household's authority.

errors.english: in cases where it was not stated that the patron would do it, or finish it, or oversee it
errors.why: The case is where the monk has not said 'I will check whether the patron has done it or finished it'; blta'o is the monk's checking, not the patron overseeing.

note: Follows the lemma-by-lemma commentary on the building pācittika, but misidentifies the cited Vinaya source and misreads several qualifications.

errors.english: what is called substance consists of two types of meaning: the external object and the consciousness
errors.why: Substance is the conditioned entity (pot etc.) that can accomplish, independently, the two kinds of purpose connected with object and cognition; substance is not divided into 'object and consciousness'.

fix.find: what is called substance consists of two types of meaning: the external object and the consciousness. These are the actual nature of conditioned things such as a flask, which arise from a collection of causes and conditions and can be established without depending on others.
fix.replace: what is called substance is the actual nature of conditioned things such as a flask, which arise from a collection of causes and conditions and can accomplish, without depending on anything else, the two kinds of purpose connected with the object and with cognition.

note: Mostly accurate on perceptibility and on sound and smell as qualities, but the definition of substance, on which the section turns, is garbled.

errors.english: If the carrier is positioned on land belonging to the boundary but has no specific purpose, there is no downfall.
errors.why: No offence where the (mantra/medicine-produced) transport does not need a carrier standing on land inside the boundary; the English makes a carrier inside the boundary blameless, contradicting the next sentence.

fix.find: If the carrier is positioned on land belonging to the boundary but has no specific purpose, there is no downfall.
fix.replace: If it does not require a carrier positioned on land belonging to the boundary, there is no downfall.

errors.english: and the value of the goods amounts to five (mashaka) a small unit of currency or more, it is a grave offense
errors.why: 'yang' (even) is lost: even when the object reaches the full five-māṣaka value (otherwise pārājika), evading customs through the air is only a sthūlātyaya.

errors.english: bypasses the customs process without attachment
errors.why: Refers to goods on which the customs levy has not been imposed (paid); 'without attachment' wrongly suggests a mental state.

errors.english: being included within the category of wasting words
errors.why: It means being included within the scope of the word 'causing loss' (ruining the owner's property), not 'wasting words'.

note: The customs-evasion casuistry is followed in outline, but the key distinctions on value and on the carrier's position are blurred.

errors.english: has not been rendered suitable for consumption by a youth
errors.why: khye'u kha 'thon pa is the third object in the list (shoots that have sprouted), joined by 'dang'; it is not the agent who renders plants allowable, and the note builds on the misreading.

note: A careful and largely accurate rendering of the five seed-types, bhūtagrāma and the definition of pāyattika.

errors.english: then regarding the claim that one might not desire all such statements, the text says:
errors.why: Both lines are one root verse ('If you say not every statement is meant, then qualify whichever is meant'); the first line is turned into commentary prose.

errors.english: establishing through the probandum should be understood in the same way as the reversal of establishing through dissimilarity
errors.why: The opponent takes 'that which establishes the probandum' as the counterpart contrasted with the establisher by dissimilarity; 'establishing through the probandum' inverts the relation.

errors.english: Similarities and dissimilarities that are erroneous [note: Tibetan: ('khrul pa); referring to fallacies of inconsistency]
errors.why: 'khrul pa here names the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason: 'similarity and dissimilarity [statements] of the inconclusive and the other pseudo-reasons'.

note: The thread of the critique of the Naiyāyika hetu definition is kept, though the verse/commentary division and some of the opponent's moves are blurred.
A faithful and well-turned rendering of the bodhisattva's verses on anger and the king's question.

errors.english: Whichever word it depends upon, one must infer "from that cause."
errors.why: gang gi sgra is 'the word "which"' (relative yad): in dependence on it, the correlative 'from that cause' is to be supplied.

fix.find: Whichever word it depends upon, one must infer "from that cause."
fix.replace: In dependence on the word "which," one must supply "from that cause."

errors.english: The phrase "at that time" should be placed first, depending on whichever word is used
errors.why: Same correlative construction: in dependence on the word 'which', 'that cause' is put in front, and the whole is construed with 'the nature of all'.

errors.english: To anticipate an objection that it possesses a specific auxiliary condition
errors.why: The whole passage from 'Even if any particular humor...' to '...auxiliary condition' is the anticipated objection introduced by 'But if the result'; the English gives its first part as the author's own view.

fix.find:
Even if any particular humor like wind were the cause, not every particular instance would possess all forms of desire and so forth. One must infer this by observing the certain result at all times.

To anticipate an objection that it possesses a specific auxiliary condition, it says: "But if the result..."
fix.replace: The objection "Even if any particular humor like wind were the cause, not every particular instance would possess all forms of desire and so forth; this is to be inferred from seeing a definite result at all times, because it has a specific auxiliary condition" is anticipated with the words "But if the result..."

errors.english: If one imagines another cause, then even smoke would not be established as having fire as its cause. The response to this is:
errors.why: That sentence is itself the reply, which the root text gives with 'smoke where fire is not seen'; it is not something being replied to.

errors.english: this relates to the object of perception
errors.why: It is a construal note: 'from which cause' is to be construed with the word 'is perceived' of the root text.

note: The humoral argument is broadly recognisable, but the commentator's syntactic glosses and the objection/reply structure are repeatedly misread.

errors.english: the observation that things like a rabbit's horns do not exist serves to prove
errors.why: It is the reason 'unproduced', which is seen in non-existents such as a rabbit's horn, that proves the subject space to be non-existent.

fix.find: the observation that things like a rabbit's horns do not exist serves to prove
fix.replace: this reason, being seen in non-existent things such as a rabbit's horn, serves to prove

errors.english: one does not necessarily have to accept every point of a treatise
errors.why: The Tibetan says that at the time of debate a treatise is simply not to be adopted; 'not necessarily' and 'every point' weaken it.

note: A good rendering of the discussion of svayam in the thesis definition, with one misconstrued example.
